content:
These arise in sequential programs that frequently read/write individual elements of nested Array/Vectors.

  1. The panicking variant of indexing (xs[i]!) constructs the default element before doing actual indexing. This can lead to unexpected slowdowns when the said default element is large (e.g. Vector \a n with large enough n). It would be nice if the default value were constructed lazily for panicking functions.

  2. Modifying an inner element involves either using xs.modify i (fun row => ...) or xs.set i (xs.get i ...) pattern. The latter tends to break linearity of the requested row, and the former, which guarantees linearity by using an unsafe body, does not exist for Vector. I use a hand-rolled Vector.modify in my code that calls out to Array.modify (it's a two-liner) and it's working great.

I've already thought about the first issue for a while. Doing it with lazy computation does unfortunately not resolve the issue in general as this means that you have to perform an allocation whenever you access the Array which yes is cheaper but still not satisfactory. Note that this construction only happens at runtime if your Inhabited value is not a closed term. Vector is unfortunately the one prominent example of a type that you might store in an array that does not have a closed term inhabited value.

The proper fix will probably be to not have Array.get! Be a runtime primitive but inline it at some point in the compilation and let the optimizer do the rest.
